title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
body:
Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms. Kairos addresses two of the biggest problems facing traditional decisioning tools: a lack of labeled data to train on and dealing with fraudsters that are constantly changing their tactics.

1. Traditional fraud solutions use ML models such as XGBoost to detect fraud, but these models are dependent on quality labeled data which many businesses do not have. We address this by using “System One” decision models in additional to traditional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. This allows you to incorporate plain language questions such as “Is this a throwaway email” into your decisioning, bypassing the need for large amounts of labeled data. This also allows you to capture aspects of fraud that are more unstructured, which is something that XGBoost models struggle with.

title: Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT
body:
Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.

Main features:

- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)

- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)

- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)

- MCP support

- Image recognition

- CRUD to your local filesystem

- Works fully offline with no internet

Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run c

title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
body:
Hey all, Kartik from Omnara (https://omnara.com) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API.

You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines.

Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an op

title: Open-source, cross-harness memory for AI agents
body:
Earlier this year, my co-founder and I found ourselves frequently switching between different coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) anytime we ran out of shaky usage limits or a newer, better model came out.

We became increasingly frustrated with having to re-explain our tasks, workflows, common mistake patterns, etc. anytime we switched agents. We found no good free alternatives out there, so we built our own and fully open-sourced it!

Beacon hooks into 20+ different agent harnesses, captures session telemetry (prompts, tool calls, command executions, etc) in one normalized format, and distills it into common patterns and repeatable workflows with a human-approval step. This compounded knowledge is then accessible to any future agent via skills / MCP.

We believe your agent data is yours to own and should not be locked behind any frontier lab's ecosystem or closed memory infrastructure. We built Beacon to make working across agents way more transparent and efficient.

Try it out and tell us what you think: https://github.com/Asymptote-Labs/agent-beacon

title: PSA: Update your Tailscale!
body:
Just a quick notice for anyone using this software in their homelab. Tailscale has released **v1.104.4** to address a series of prominent vulnerabilities [disclosed last week](https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/unpatched-tailscale-ssh-flaws-could-let.html). These vulns affect the [Tailscale Serve](https://tailscale.com/docs/features/tailscale-serve) and [Tailscale SSH](https://tailscale.com/docs/features/tailscale-ssh) functionalities of the software, and allow already-authorized attackers to gain further privileges erroneously. Kindly update to that version or higher, especially if you are using one of the SSH/Serve features.

For [headscale](https://headscale.net/) selfhosters that also use Tailscale SSH, consider setting `TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1` on all clients, as headscale does not have a way to force turning off SSH forwarding (one of the attack vectors). Headscale also has a relevant disclosed vulnerability affecting node registration, and an in-progress patch for that which is trackable [here](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/pull/3586/).

Finally, do give your SSH grants/access control list a review again. You may also disable these ssh/serve features if you don't

On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.

The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies.

title: Open Source OS That Are Not Linux

Every system listed below is open source and not powered by Linux. Each has an ISO or installer you can boot today, and many of the picks can even run Linux applications.

Think of it as a list of operating systems that are friends with Tux but not friendly enough to call him inside for a cup of tea.

This list is not ranked.

Vinix

If you own an Apple Silicon MacBook and want a system that is neither macOS nor a Linux distribution, Vinix is aimed at you. Only the original M1 is supported today, and Alexander Medvednikov, the author of V, maintains the project.

The kernel is monolithic and written mostly in V, while part of it is C and assembly. Because memory is managed by hand, no garbage collector can interrupt a system call, and the security model borrows certain concepts from OpenBSD.

On ARM64, it runs Alpine Linux binaries natively, and pkg installs packages from Alpine's aarch64 repositories. ISOs for both x86-64 and ARM64 are available for virtual machine use.

A good pick if you enjoy poking at experimental kernels.

title: AlpineBSD announced – an AI-free FOSS OS
body:
Just days after Daemonarchy, there's another new OS in the BSD family – and one that is heading determinedly in almost the opposite direction.

AlpineBSD is so new that it barely exists yet. There are no installation media available, though it's possible to manually bootstrap an installation. What AlpineBSD does already have is an AI policy, and the plan is to avoid "the output of generative AI models (e.g. LLMs)" as far as possible:

"Any software whose code, documentation, binaries, or other assets include, in any part, the output of a generative AI tool such as an LLM, is considered 'tainted' for our purposes."

The core idea is to combine the kernel of NetBSD with "a userspace inspired by Alpine Linux and the objective of making it possible to use as little AI-generated software as possible."

Back in 2024, the NetBSD project made its position on AI plain. Its commit guidelines say that "code generated by a Large Language Model […] is presumed to be tainted code."

Back in July, Linus Torvalds stated that "Linux is not one of those anti-AI projects". Since then, NetBSD has seen a spike in donations and interest.

title: Wine on OpenBSD? Yes, and It Can Already Run The Witcher 3
body:
A bit of a surprise, really, Wine is making its way to OpenBSD. An experimental port has been submitted, and early testing shows it can already run dozens of 64-bit Windows apps (including quite a few games).

The announcement comes from OpenBSD developer Thomas Frohwein, who made the proposed port public on the OpenBSD mailing list and describes it as possibly the most surprising port proposal of the year.

As Frohwein makes clear, getting Wine to work on OpenBSD has been a team effort with the bulk of the work being done by Andrii and Fabien. The biggest hurdle has been the %gs segment register. Wine needs this, but OpenBSD doesn’t allow applications to set GSBASE directly.

The breakthrough was a software workaround which uses the %gs prefix to generate the instructions, circumventing a major compatibility issue which had previously made getting Wine onto the OS so difficult.

The results are already very impressive. The dev team has successfully tested a good number of 64-bit Windows apps, and most run quite nicely. Even more surprisingly, a recent remaster of The Witcher 3 appears to run quite well (though again you do need to install vkd3d-proton to get the D3D12 via Vulkan t

title: ReactOS Can Now Be Installed & Used With Its NTFS Driver
body:
The ReactOS open-source operating system has seen its NTFS file-system driver mature to the point that it can be finally used for installing and using ReactOS with it. NTFS formatting support is also finally now possible with this driver too.

Hitting this major milestone of its NTFS driver maturing to the point of installing and using the ReactOS operating system itself with it also puts the project one step closer to its elusive beta release.

ReactOS posted to X today this big goal being realized of the NTFS driver being much more mature for handling ReactOS installations.

It is important to note though that the ReactOS NTFS driver still lacks caching leading to slower performance than other NTFS drivers/platforms, journaling, and security support are also not yet implemented. There is also the possibility of other undiscovered bugs they note.

A nice milestone for ReactOS and the latest in a variety of nice achievements they have made so far in 2026.

title: Let's Encrypt to Cut SSL Certificate Lifetimes to 64 Days in February 2027
body:
Let’s Encrypt, the free and open certificate authority widely used to secure websites with HTTPS, announced it will shorten the default validity period of its TLS certificates from 90 days to 64 days, starting February 10, 2027.

All certificates issued or renewed from that date will have a 64-day lifespan unless users explicitly select one of the shorter options already available: 45 or six days.

Existing certificates will remain valid until their expiration dates. Let’s Encrypt expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The organization also confirmed no valid certificates will be revoked during the transition.

To help administrators prepare, Let’s Encrypt will introduce 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026, allowing users to test their renewal setups before the change reaches production.

The move is part of a broader effort to improve web security by reducing how long compromised or incorrectly issued certificates remain usable. Simply put, shorter certificate lifetimes mean attackers have less time to exploit a stolen private key.

Unveiling the design, TDF’s Italo Vignoli made the case for a decoupling of the two brands, noting “the foundation speaks as an institution, not as a software project” whose work “extends well beyond the product” that it’s known for, i.e. LibreOffice.


Design breakout

URA Design, a Berlin-based design agency whose former clients include Mozilla and the Tor Project, handled the redesign. Its founder also worked on Ubuntu’s desktop installer in the past.
Trivia: Canonical went the other way during its last brand revamp, incorporating the Ubuntu logo in to the Canonical wordmark, replacing its old, separate logo of two nested purple circles.

Carving out a visual identity of its own feels somewhat overdue.

title: Denmark’s Collabora Pilot Was Never The Microsoft Replacement

Collabora has published its own account of the Danish ministry pilot that earlier coverage, including ours, had described as Denmark moving off Microsoft's office software.

The ministry's own launch release had described it as a test by a group of employees in one department. Back then, the minister handling this, Caroline Stage Olsen, had said the tech giants were not being tossed out the door overnight.

A volunteer test, not a switch

The pilot began in June 2025, when volunteers in the Danish digitalization ministry's own department started writing documents in Collabora instead of Microsoft's Word, Excel, and PowerPoint editors.

cBrain, the Danish company behind the ministry's F2 case and document management system, was tasked with integrating Collabora into it.

The ministry presented it as a test from the beginning and said that a wider rollout in the department depended on the results. Days later, it told Version2 (in Danish) that no decision to phase out Microsoft had been made and that the plan was not to replace Windows with Linux.

title: LiberNT: New ReactOS Fork Aims for Windows 11 Compatibility
body:
The LiberNT project is working on an alternative implementation of the Windows NT architecture, using Windows 11 version 24H2 as its compatibility reference. Unlike Linux distributions, LiberNT does not use the Linux kernel. It builds on the ReactOS codebase while replacing and extending several core components.

One of the project’s main priorities is ARM64 support, particularly for single-board computers and embedded devices. LiberNT also supports x86-64 and 32-bit x86, while RISC-V 64-bit and PowerPC ports are under development.

According to the developers, the implementation follows a clean-room approach. Windows behavior is studied using Microsoft’s public documentation, SDK and WDK headers, public symbols, and black-box testing. The team states no proprietary Windows code is copied or transcribed.

On the technical side, one of the biggest changes is NVS, a new memory manager and kernel pool implementation replacing the corresponding ReactOS components. LiberNT also introduces a new cache manager, with developers claiming better results than the original ReactOS memory manager in their memory and cache benchmarks.

Other changes include a new NTFS driver, an updated StorPort

title: Are you from Germany? We need you 🇩🇪
body:
Germans are great. Especially when they do nice things.

A lot of German people contribute to open-source projects in their spare time – unpaid, often for years.  And yet, under Germany's tax law, this work is not recognized as volunteer work (Ehrenamt) – unlike club work, youth work, or emergency services.

A petition to the German Bundestag's petitions committee is calling for equal treatment. 

Concretely, this would mean:

🔴 Tax-free expense allowances (Ehrenamts-/Übungsleiterpauschale)

⚪ Easier non-profit status (§52 AO) for open-source projects

🟢  Better liability protection for open source maintainers (analogous to §31a BGB)

🔵 Legally secure donation receipts and cost reimbursement

This would be a huge boost to the open source community.

**Petition:**  https://www.openpetition.de/petition/online/anerkennung-von-open-source-arbeit-als-ehrenamt-in-deutschland

Please sign it.  It only takes 2 minutes.

If you're not in Germany, sharing it with people who are would still help a lot.

Thank you 🙏

title: I built a free and open-source desktop app for organizing table tennis tournaments
body:
Hi! I’m a table tennis player, club captain and referee who apparently decided that what the world desperately needed was another tournament manager.

So I made LibreTT. 🏓

It’s a desktop app for running table tennis tournaments: players, registrations, fees, groups, draws, matches, knockout brackets, results, backups and exports. It runs on Linux, Windows and macOS, works offline and requires no account.

So why another one?

Because I don’t think competition data should belong to the software that records it.

A result is created by players, clubs, referees and organizers. The software is just a tool. If LibreTT disappears tomorrow, your tournament history shouldn’t disappear with it.

That’s why LibreTT is licensed under AGPL-3.0-or-later. No subscriptions, activation servers, paid feature tiers or vendor lock-in. The source is public, the data stays local, and the community should always be able to preserve, move and continue its own infrastructure.

This is the first public beta (0.1.0-beta.1), so the next milestone is testing it against its natural predator: an actual tournament organizer who is 15 minutes behind schedule.

title: Court Agrees with EFF: Utah’s VPN Law Demands a Technical Impossibility
body:
When state lawmakers attempt to rewrite how the internet works, users rely on courts to recognize that laws can’t make technical impossibilities a reality. That’s why we were happy to see that a court has blocked Utah’s attempt to outlaw the privacy protections of Virtual Private Networks (VPNs). 

In a win for digital rights, a federal judge has issued a preliminary injunction blocking Utah’s SB 73, the state’s draconian anti-VPN age verification law. The decision comes as EFF submitted our comments to the Utah Department of Commerce, detailing how forcing platforms to detect and block privacy-preserving tools undermines user privacy and security worldwide while demanding the impossible.  
What SB 73 Does 

Signed into law earlier this year, SB 73 attempted to regulate adult websites by requiring them to block VPN users or to identify the physical location of visitors using them or similar tools that mask their network traffic. It even went so far as to prohibit websites from offering instructions on how to use a VPN to bypass these checks. This made Utah, to EFF’s knowledge, the first state in the nation to target the use of VPNs to avoid legally mandated age-verification gates.

EFF brought a lawsuit against the US government over social media AI powered mass surveilence. The Government tried to dismiss the suit on multiple grounds. Lack of standing, lack of of injury, pre-enforcement, and others.

The EFF prevailed on every point. The suit against the administration can go forward. Whether EFF prevails on the merits of the case, we will see. But it is a good start. The court was sympathetic to the EFF's arguments so far.

> The court disagreed, explaining that “Plaintiffs’ allegations are of an ongoing surveillance program that is actively chilling the speech of their members and otherwise causing harm.” That chilling effect is a First Amendment injury even if there isn’t a direct prohibition on speech. And when government conduct is actively chilling speech right now, a challenge to it isn’t pre-enforcement. 

Please resist the pull of thinking that even if the EFF wins the case, it is useless b/c it does not solve *every* privacy problem. We will never have a single nail to strike with a single hammer. There are many battles in the war for privacy. The more won, the better.

The Axios investigation cited people familiar with the matter who said some banks were aware of unauthorized access involving AI agents. In certain cases, the tools contacted bank call centers or appeared to perform tasks that customers had not specifically requested.

title: Require Police to Get a Warrant to Search ALPR Data
body:
> Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are mass surveillance. They photograph every passing car and log where and when it was captured, building a searchable record of where nearly everyone drives. Cities should not buy them, and cities that already have them should shut them down.
> 
> Where these systems still operate, courts and state legislatures must reduce their harms by (among other things) requiring police to get a warrant before searching stored ALPR data. A warrant requirement would not make mass surveillance acceptable, but it would require police to justify a search to a judge before accessing records of people’s movements. Without this independent judicial check on police power, officers have been searching this data for improper reasons (many exposed by EFF) that violate our fundamental rights.

title: Killed by Ubuntu, Linux Mint is Bringing This Classic Feature Back
body:
Okay, killed by Ubuntu is an exaggeration, as Ubuntu is not the only Linux distro doing this.

Still, the big news is that Linux Mint is bringing hibernation back.

In a recent blog post, the Mint team previewed a new Sleep Modes page in the System Administration tool. It's meant to make enabling hibernation and setting it up correctly easy, without you editing config files by hand. The feature is planned for the upcoming Mint 27 release coming in December.

Mint hasn't magically fixed the problems that made Ubuntu drop hibernation. What it does is give you the choice, along with two hybrid modes that sit between suspend and hibernation.

Hibernation vs suspend: What's the difference?

Both features are about saving your session, which simply means everything you have open like your apps, windows and documents.

When you suspend (also called sleep), your computer keeps your session in RAM and powers down almost everything else. Waking up takes a couple of seconds. The catch is that RAM needs power to hold that data, so a suspended laptop keeps draining its battery.

If the battery dies while suspended, your session is lost, along with any unsaved work.

title: Linux Mint Devs Introduce New System Monitor and Terminal Emulator Apps // The devs also introduced the Unfold archive manager and added a preview pane in the Nemo file manager.
body:
The Linux Mint devs keep working on new features and apps for the upcoming Linux Mint 27 “Adrien” release, due out in Christmas 2026, and they just unveiled new system monitor, terminal emulator, and archive manager tools today.

Meet Superlight, a new system monitor app for Linux Mint that features graphs for CPU, RAM, swap, GPU, network, disk I/O, temperature, and fan speed. The app shows how much of the system’s resources each application uses, and the same data is available for all running processes, with a large variety of columns you can sort and reorder.

On laptops, the Superlight system monitor app shows battery status and a history of charge level and power input/output. The Storage page breaks down disk usage and lets you browse the files and folders that take up the most space, as well as Steam games and Flatpak apps.

Another new app is Velocitty, a simple terminal emulator that comes with a tab overview and can be themed with palettes. Tabs can be reordered, moved between terminal windows, or detached into a new window. Also, tab colors can be changed to show red for superuser sessions, blue for remote sessions, and a lighter shade for running processes.

I’d like to use an offline vector map (not bitmap) with more or less up-to-date map data on my Windows Mobile 6 Professional (Windows CE-based,  not  related to Windows Phone) device. (These devices typically have only 64 MiB RAM, which constraints them quite a bit.) 
 
  OpenStreetMap would be nice, but I’d not say no to commercial solutions.

title: Alternative to Docker Content Trust (and cosign)?
body:
Does anyone have a good recommendation to an alternative to Docker Content Trust, ideally where the developer themselves holds the private release signing key? 
 State of DCT 
 By default, docker security is a nightmare -- esspecially on ephemeral CI runners, where  DCT is 100% security theater . 
 We've been using  DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1  and  rsync to manually pin the keys  for the debian image layers we download with  docker pull . This had the effect of disabling TOFU. That's important because, if we don't pin the certificates manually with rsync, then docker would happily pull a malicious image (and the malicious singing keys at the same time, from mallory). By pinning the keys before ever running  docker pull , that's the only way we can get docker to detect a malicious image (not signed by the key we expect) on an ephemeral build machine. 
 Unfortunately, I just discovered that the official docker documentation says that DCT is being deprecated. Apparently this was announced last year, and in June this blog post was published with advice: 
 
  https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-content-trust-retirement-and-migration-guidance/  
 
 Cosign is not secure

body:
Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic (https://simantic.com). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware.

Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes.

We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago.

title: Show HN: AstroHelm – Use your phone camera to aim a telescope or telephoto lens
body:
Hello HN!

As an amateur astronomer living in New York City, finding objects in the night sky has always been a huge challenge. I thought about using the smartphone's gyroscope and magnetometer, but the accuracy left a lot to be desired.

Then I learned about plate solving: given a picture of the sky, we can determine exactly where in the sky the camera was pointing by identifying the star pattern. This was a much better fit - as long as the phone and the optics are rigidly connected, we can repeatedly photograph the sky and determine the pointing direction with very high accuracy.

A lot of work was done to design an algorithm that works reliably with smartphone cameras, which have limited light sensitivity and wider field of view which includes buildings and trees. I experimented a lot with machine learning, and to my surprise, traditional CV methods actually performed better at extracting stars from the image.

The result is AstroHelm, an iOS and Android app that helps figure out where your telescope or camera is pointing, and guides you to the object of your choice. Just follow an arrow on screen, and the object will land right in your eyepiece or viewfinder. Everythin

title: Show HN: Certo – An open source platform to deliver Open Badges
body:
Certo is open-source infrastructure for issuing, managing, verifying, and exchanging digital credentials.

It implements Open Badges 3.0[1] and W3C Verifiable Credentials[2] which are the open standards that make credentials portable, machine-verifiable, and vendor-independent.

It is designed to be:

- Self-hosted: run it inside your own infrastructure, air-gapped network, or sovereign cloud - Standards-compliant: credentials it issues work with any OB3/VC-compatible system - API-first: everything the UI can do, the API can do - Exportable: your data is always yours, in open formats - Extensible: a small, stable core with a plugin interface for everything else

A demo is available at https://certo.schroedinger-hat.org/ which we're using for Schrödinger Hat[3] conferences, workshops, partner communities.

I'll be around if you have any questions. Feel free to give a feedback on the project.

[1] https://www.imsglobal.org/spec/ob/v3p0 [2]

body:
Hi HN, we're the founders of Salem Robotics (https://salemroboticsinc.com). We give existing mobile robots the task-specific intelligence to carry out surveys and physically interactive inspections in hazardous industrial facilities.

Here's a video of it running on real robot hardware with a few words from us: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U_228h3NE7c

We came to Salem through robotics research at UT Austin and a combined 15 years working in nuclear, including about 10 years developing and deploying autonomous robots at Los Alamos National Laboratory. title: Create, preview, and edit files directly in the Gemini app
body: We’re introducing new ways to create and refine files and code in the Gemini app. You can now generate, preview, and edit files right within your Gemini app chat—expand to full screen to type edits directly, highlight text to ask questions, or have Gemini refine them. PDF preview and editing is supported on both the web and mobile, while all other formats (documents, spreadsheets, slide decks, Markdown files, TXT files, and code) are supported on the web only. Here are just some of the new things you can do:      Generate and refine slide decks:  Create presentation outlines or slide content, preview the layout in chat, and edit directly or ask Gemini to adjust the tone and structure before opening in Google Slides, or downloading as a PPTX or PDF.   Build and export Google Sheets:  Generate structured trackers, tables, and data models from a prompt, preview them in Gemini, and open them directly in Google Sheets.   Edit documents and PDFs:  Quickly draft PDFs, Google Docs, LaTeX, Markdown, or TXT files, and make manual or prompted edits inline on web or in a full-screen view—plus you can upload all of them to Drive. body: We’re introducing a library of  immersive explorations  in the Gemini app, giving users an interactive, visual way to explore topics layer-by-layer, from microscopic systems to deep space. Users can access this library in the  Gemini student hub  by clicking on “Try immersive explorations” and will soon be able to access  these immersive explorations  directly in a chat conversation with Gemini.  Whether it’s tracing trade routes on the Silk Road, peering inside a jet engine, or studying the physics of lightning, each scene unfolds into interactive nodes with guided explanations. Users can tap a layer to dig deeper, journeying from sweeping planetary scales straight down to molecules and atoms. Immersive explorations will soon include audio narration to walk users through each layer.  This feature is available on web and mobile to all users in the following languages: English, Indonesian, Hindi, Brazilian Portuguese, French, and simplified Chinese. This cell-level source attribution gives you full visibility to audit, verify, and cross-reference outputs for greater trust and accuracy. title: Create box and whisker charts in Google Sheets
body: Google Sheets now natively supports box and whisker charts, a statistical chart type that shows how a dataset is distributed. Select a range of raw numeric values and Sheets calculates the minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum, mean, and outliers for you, with no helper formulas needed. You can choose inclusive or exclusive quartile calculation and show or hide inner points, outliers, mean markers, and mean lines.  Box and whisker support also comes with enhanced Microsoft Excel import compatibility. Previously, importing Excel files containing box and whisker charts into Sheets would drop the chart entirely. Now, these charts are preserved on import with their data references, calculations, and formatting intact, and charts created in Sheets export back to Excel as editable box and whisker charts. title: Amazon Connect Customer lets agents pause and resume emails
body:
Amazon Connect Customer lets agents pause emails while waiting for information or approvals, freeing them to handle higher-priority contacts and resume their work later. For example, an agent waiting for a supervisor to approve a refund can pause the email and take an incoming call. Paused time is tracked separately from active handling time, giving supervisors a more accurate view of the time agents spend working on emails.  
 Agents can pause and resume emails directly from the Agent Workspace or Contact Control Panel (CCP) and see how long each email has been paused. Supervisors can monitor paused emails and pause duration in real time, and use flows to automatically resume or transfer emails that remain paused beyond a configured threshold.  
 Amazon Connect Customer email pause and resume is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London)  regions . To learn more and get started, please refer to the help  documentation  or visit the  Amazon Connect Customer  website.

title: Amazon WorkSpaces for AI agents now supports Linux and Windows 11 cloud desktops
body:
WorkSpaces for AI agents now supports Linux and Windows 11 cloud desktops, in addition to Windows Server. You can run each AI agent on the operating system that its workflows and applications require. Your agents can then work in the same environments that your workforce already uses, without re-platforming.   
 Linux desktops give agents full root access to the operating system where many developers already build, test, and automate agentic workflows. Agents can take on developer tasks, such as running builds, tests, and scripts, within the enterprise-grade security and governance controls you already rely on. Windows 11 desktops let agents work in the enterprise applications your teams depend on every day.  
 Linux and Windows 11 desktops have the same security and governance controls as Windows Server desktops. These include network isolation, IAM-based access, and the compliance boundaries your organization already has in place.  
 To get started operating AI agents on WorkSpaces, visit:  https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appstream2/latest/developerguide/agent-access.html .

title: Amazon RDS now supports the latest Cumulative Update and GDR updates for Microsoft SQL Server
body:

We recommend that you upgrade your Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances to apply these updates using Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. You can learn more about upgrading your database instance in the  Amazon RDS SQL Server User Guide for upgrading your RDS Microsoft SQL Server DB engine .

title: AWS Transform for mainframe improves the reimagine modernization workflow
body:
AWS Transform for mainframe now discovers business functions with field-level precision and generates a new requirements coverage report in the assess and reimagine workflow. Previously, business functions that used the same table or file were grouped together, and you had to build your own traceability reporting from AWS Transform artifacts. With this launch, you can start modernizing z/OS COBOL and PL/I workloads from a more accurate catalog of business functions and verify requirements coverage before you build. 
 Business functions are now grouped only when they affect the same data fields. They also include screens and queues and carry clearer names and descriptions. The new requirements coverage report shows how every part of your application is accounted for in the generated requirements. Every line of source code is classified by how it was handled, every business rule links to the exact lines it came from, and every requirement is backed by the business rules that support it. You can review coverage from the full portfolio down to a single line before moving into forward engineering in Kiro and other IDEs.

title: Amazon EKS Capabilities now supports Argo CD Notifications
body:

You define triggers and message templates in your cluster and subscribe individual Applications with an annotation, the same way you do in upstream Argo CD.  
 With this launch, you can deliver notifications to 16 notification services, including Slack, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Amazon SQS, and Amazon EventBridge. The Amazon SQS and Amazon EventBridge services authenticate with your IAM Capability Role, so you can route deployment events into your own event-driven workflows without storing credentials in your cluster. For a service that requires third-party credentials such as a Slack token, you can specify an AWS Secrets Manager ARN in place of the secret and EKS will automatically use it on your behalf.

title: Haiku 5.5 now available on Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US)
body:

 Claude Haiku 5.5 is the fastest model in the Claude 5.5 family. It's a clear step up from Claude Haiku 4.5, built for work that runs in large volumes and needs quick responses. Developers can use it to summarize and compact long context, classify and route requests, process text in bulk, and make small, targeted edits across many files. It also works well as a review subagent that runs in parallel, while Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 take on harder planning and coding work. Haiku 5.5 uses adaptive thinking across five effort levels from low to max, with medium as the default. It's available with a 1M context window and a 0.06x credit multiplier. Requests over 100K tokens are billed at a 0.3x multiplier.  
 Ensure your IDE or CLI is updated to the latest version, then restart it to access the new model from the model selector. For more details, visit the  GovCloud documentation , the  monitoring and tracking guide , or contact your AWS account team. To learn more about Kiro, visit the  Kiro product

title: Amazon RDS now supports per snapshot billing
body:
Starting today, Amazon RDS supports per snapshot billing for Amazon RDS snapshots. Per snapshot billing allows you to get the cost of each individual snapshot.  
 Previously, RDS snapshot charges were aggregated at the database instance level on the Cost and Usage report as well as the Cost Explorer. This meant that while understanding the snapshot charges, you could only see the aggregate view at the database instance instead of drilling down to each individual snapshot. Now, you can use cost allocation tags on your snapshots to see exactly how much each snapshot costs, giving you a better understanding of your backups spend and budgets. Per snapshot billing is enabled by default on all RDS snapshots for no additional charge.  
 Per snapshot billing is available for all Amazon RDS engines in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, please visit our  documentation .

title: Amazon Quick on desktop now uses your organization's existing Amazon Quick sign-in
body:
For organizations that use Amazon Quick, the desktop application now signs users in with the same sign-in method the organization already uses for Quick on the web. Administrators no longer need to register an OIDC application in their identity provider or set up separate desktop sign-in before users can get started. If a user can sign in to Quick on the web, that user can sign in to the desktop application.  
 To turn on desktop access, an administrator adds the desktop connector once in the Amazon Quick console. Users then enter their Quick account name, choose Sign In, and finish signing in through their browser. This works for accounts that use IAM Identity Center, IAM federation, or native Amazon Quick users. If your organization wants to manage desktop sign-in separately, you can still set up a dedicated identity provider configuration with providers such as Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Okta, or Ping Identity.  
 Amazon Quick on desktop is available in  AWS Regions that support the full Amazon Quick feature set .  
 To get started, see  Amazon Quick on desktop  in the Amazon Quick User Guide.

AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources
body:
AWS Lambda now supports  queues for Apache Kafka  in  self-managed Kafka event source mappings  (ESM), for Kafka clusters that customers run themselves and for managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. Customers can now scale processing for Kafka workloads beyond the partition count of a topic, increasing throughput during traffic spikes and improving processing resilience.  
 Customers building event-driven Kafka workloads for use cases such as image and video encoding, fraud detection, notification delivery, and telemetry ingestion treat each event as an independent unit of work, where processing speed matters more than strict ordering. Previously, Kafka ESMs used the Kafka consumer group protocol, which assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within a consumer group. Customers needing higher parallelism had to over-partition topics or move traffic to a separate queuing system, adding infrastructure to operate and producer code to maintain. Queue support for self-managed Kafka ESMs is built on Kafka share groups, which are generally available in Apache Kafka 4.2. title: Amazon Aurora MySQL 3.14 (compatible with MySQL 8.0.46) is generally available
body:
Starting today, Amazon Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition 3 (compatible with MySQL 8.0) supports MySQL 8.0.46, which includes community MySQL fixes and Aurora-specific improvements. In addition to operational improvements, Aurora MySQL 3.14 introduces support for post-quantum TLS (PQ-TLS) key exchange, providing you with post-quantum cryptography options for encrypting your data in-transit. For detailed information on this release, refer to  Aurora MySQL 3  and  MySQL 8.0.46  release notes.  
 You can upgrade your databases during scheduled maintenance windows using automatic minor version upgrades. To simplify operations at scale, enable  automatic minor version upgrades  and use the AWS Organizations  Upgrade Rollout Policy  to orchestrate upgrades across your clusters in phases. You can perform minor version upgrades in-place or via snapshot restore. This release is supported in all  AWS Regions  where Aurora MySQL is available.  
  Amazon Aurora  is designed for high performance and availability at global scale with full MySQL compatibility. It provides scale-to-zero serverless compute, Aurora Global Database for multi-Region resilience, Aurora I/O-Optimized for improved price per

title: Amazon Connect Customer now supports Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools in flows
body:
Amazon Connect Customer now enables you to invoke Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools in customer experience flows through the new 'External Tool' block. With this launch, you can connect flows to third-party applications through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway and reuse the same tools used by your agentic experiences to retrieve data or trigger actions, without writing custom Lambda functions. For example, when a customer contacts a financial institution about a recent transaction, a flow can use the External Tool block to retrieve relevant context from a third-party application, such as case history from their CRM system, or transaction details from a banking platform.  
 This feature is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more about this feature, refer to the  administrator guide . To learn more about Amazon Connect Customer, an agentic AI solution that helps enterprises deliver exceptional customer experiences, visit the  Amazon Connect Customer website.

title: Amazon Connect Customer now supports Cases and External Tool events in the Wait block
body:
Amazon Connect Customer now supports Cases and External Tool events in the Wait block, giving you more control over how your customer experience flows react to real-time data changes. In addition to waiting for a Lambda function to complete, you can now wait until a Connect Case field meets a specified condition or an External Tool invocation completes. This enables you to wait for critical information before advancing an interaction, reducing unnecessary transfers and saving time for both your end-customers and agents. For example, you can hold a flow until a refund status field is updated on a case, then automatically resume and route the interaction based on the outcome.   
 To learn more about this feature, refer to the  administrator guide  and availability of  Connect Customer features by Region . To learn more about Amazon Connect Customer, an agentic AI solution that helps enterprises deliver exceptional customer experiences, visit the  Amazon Connect Customer website.

title: EC2 Amazon Machine Images can now be scanned for vulnerabilities through Amazon Inspector
body:
Amazon Inspector now extends its vulnerability scanning to EC2 Amazon Machine Images (AMIs), enabling you to identify software vulnerabilities in your AMIs without launching instances or installing additional software. This helps you fix issues at the source before AMIs are used to launch instances across your fleet.  
 With this capability, you can run continuous evaluations to monitor your AMI catalog for newly discovered vulnerabilities, or perform targeted one-time scans for specific AMIs directly from the EC2 Console. You can enable AMI scanning for an account or across your entire organization in Amazon Inspector. For AWS Security Hub customers, you can enable AMI scanning as an add-on across your organization, and findings are also delivered to Security Hub. Based on the scan results, you can enable the  Allowed AMIs  setting and specify security criteria that AMIs must meet to be available within your account and enforce this setting across the entire organization using Declarative Policies. Customers building AMIs with  EC2 Image Builder  can integrate scanning directly into their pipelines and restrict distribution of AMIs that do not meet their security standards.
