title: Souborový systém ZFS: přechod a běžná práce s daty
body: Chtěli byste začít se souborovým systémem ZFS, ale už používáte nějaký jiný a nechce se vám instalovat systém od začátku? Ukážeme si, jak je možné přejít na ZFS pohodlně a zachovat všechna důležitá data.

title: Softwarová sklizeň (4. 11. 2026): poštovní server s kalendáři a kontakty
body: Sonda do světa svobodného softwaru. Dnes si připojíme sluchátka Nothing a CMF, vyzkoušíme odlehčený hudební přehrávač pro Linux, řekneme si o experimentálním terminálovém emulátoru pro KDE a podíváme se na jeden poštovní server.

title: Americké sankce jako varování: jak snížit závislost evropského internetu?
body: Evropský internet může působit jako decentralizovaná síť, jeho provoz však v praxi závisí na službách, firmách a institucích soustředěných v několika zemích. Jak velké je toto riziko a co s ním mohou udělat provozovatelé?

title: Využití textur ve WebGL a OpenGL ES: zvětšování, zmenšování a blending
body: V sedmém článku o technologiích WebGL a OpenGL ES si popíšeme další možnosti, které nabízí texturovací subsystém Open GL ES. Popíšeme si filtraci textur při jejich zvětšování a/nebo zmenšování a využití blendingu.

title: Postřehy z bezpečnosti: zmizení krypta za rekordních 6,3 miliard dolarů
body: V tomto vydání Postřehů se podíváme na rekordní krádež 6,3 miliardy dolarů z Binance, AI zneužitou při útoku na Chainalysis i v podvrženém rozšíření Claude Code a kritickou chybu v linuxovém jádře.

title: OpenAlt 2026: technologie, které dávají svobodu
body: Jak fungují technologie, které používáme každý den? Je možné mít kontrolu nad vlastním telefonem, daty a soukromím? Co všechno lze vytvořit s otevřeným softwarem, vlastním hardwarem nebo pomocí vzájemně si pomáhajících lidí?

title: Vývoj SVT-AV2 běží naplno, nový nástroj FlashRAW

title: Linuxové jádro 7.4 přijde s podporu Steam Frame a zrychlením FAT32

title: Nintendo Switch 2: Mario, myš a porty, co se dřív neodvažovaly
body: Switch 2 má rychlejší menu, ale hlavně rychlejší hry. Mario Kart World vás probudí líp než espresso, Fast Fusion ukazuje technický strop a Cyberpunk 2077 je port, který by ještě nedávno zněl jako městská legenda.

title: Micro: až překvapivě kvalitní textový editor
body: V Linuxu je k dispozici takřka nepřeberné množství různých textových editorů. Dnes se seznámíme s editorem nazvaným mikro, jenž kombinuje přehledné ovládání s pokročilejšími operacemi: více oken, makra a pluginy.

title: Příliv čínských balíčků do Česka dál vysychá. Dovoz se propadl na sedminu, a to ještě před novým poplatkem
body: Zatímco v neděli začala Evropa vybírat nový poplatek za zásilky ze třetích zemí, už ten předchozí dokázal řadu nakupujících odradit. Podle nejnovějších dat počet položek proudících do Česka v říjnu klesl na sedminu toho, co bylo běžné loni.

title: Zatímco se kvůli AI propouští, česká firma díky ní raketově roste. Tržby míří na miliardy a cílí na stovky milionů uživatelů
body: Před rokem pár stovek milionů, dnes skoro dvě miliardy. Česká firma Apify se se správným nastavením nachází ve správném čase na správném místě.

title: Firmy v Česku už kvůli AI nenabírají, nebo rovnou propouštějí. Přestože chápou, že junioři dojdou

title: Česko se rozhoupalo a podpořilo velký evropský plán na podporu technologických firem. Mezitím z něj zbyl slepenec mnoha zájmů

title: If you're on a Pixel 9 or 10, is the Pixel 11 worth it to you?
body:
Been comparing the Pixel 9/10/11 and the gap is smaller than the marketing makes it sound, so curious what others think.

The way I read it: same 6.3in body all three years. The 9 actually has the biggest main sensor but no zoom lens. The 10 added a 5x zoom and the magnetic Qi2 charging but shrank the main camera. The 11 keeps the zoom, brings a bigger main sensor back, and bumps wireless to 25W. None of the base three get a vapor chamber, so they all throttle in long games.

My take: on a 10 I wouldn't bother; on a 9 the zoom + magnets + faster wireless are the things you'd feel daily.

For the Pixel 9 and 10 owners here — has the camera or charging actually pushed anyone to upgrade, or is it a "wait for the 12" year?

title: LibreOffice Hits 9.4 Million Downloads in Just Eight Weeks
body:
>LibreOffice continues to enjoy strong demand following the release of version 26.8 in August. According to new figures from The Document Foundation, the open-source office suite recorded 9.4 million downloads over eight weeks, from August 24 to October 18, averaging more than one million downloads per week.
>
>Even more impressive, LibreOffice’s total downloads for 2026 have already surpassed the entire 2025 figure, with ten weeks still remaining in the year.
>
>The latest numbers follow the record-breaking first week of LibreOffice 26.8, which saw 1,031,162 downloads shortly after release. Before the announcement, weekly downloads were slightly below one million but have remained above since.
>
>And those 9.4 million downloads don’t tell the whole story. TDF explains that Windows updates are counted separately, as are downloads of older LibreOffice versions, which also continue to attract considerable interest.
>

title: France’s Weird Per-Gigabyte Data Tax Could Cost VLC Over €1 Million a Year!
body:
> At least that's what VLC thinks when protesting the new French law.
> 
> France's National Assembly has voted in favour of a new "internet tax" that would charge companies for every gigabyte of data they send to users in France.
> 
> The idea is to make Netflix, Google, Meta and the rest of Big Tech pay more.
> 
> That sounds like a dream come true for many of us who prefer taking ownership of data in our own hands but unfortunately things are not that simple.
> 
> The way this law is written, it doesn't stop at Big Tech. Even VLC, a free and open source media player maintained by a non-profit, could end up paying this new tax.
> What the new French internet tax says
> New French Internet Tax law
> 
> The measure is amendment I-1358 to France's 2027 finance bill, tabled by Laurent Lhardit. It creates a tax on "producers of digital data" at €0.055 (5.5 euro cents) for every gigabyte delivered to subscribers of French internet providers.
> 
> Internet providers would measure how much data each sender pushes to their customers, with the collection supervised by telecom regulator Arcep and the tax administration DGFiP. Only the volume is counted, not the content or where it goes.

It’s a fascinating piece of work, a flying wing uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) is designed parametrically in FreeCAD. Eleven parameters are broken out which control the wing geometry and these are automatically adjusted. title: Wine on OpenBSD? Yes, and It Can Already Run The Witcher 3
body:

>

>

title: Let's Encrypt to Cut SSL Certificate Lifetimes to 64 Days in February 2027
body:
>Let’s Encrypt, the free and open certificate authority widely used to secure websites with HTTPS, announced it will shorten the default validity period of its TLS certificates from 90 days to 64 days, starting February 10, 2027.
>
>All certificates issued or renewed from that date will have a 64-day lifespan unless users explicitly select one of the shorter options already available: 45 or six days.
>
>Existing certificates will remain valid until their expiration dates. Let’s Encrypt expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The organization also confirmed no valid certificates will be revoked during the transition.
>
>To help administrators prepare, Let’s Encrypt will introduce 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026, allowing users to test their renewal setups before the change reaches production.
>
>The move is part of a broader effort to improve web security by reducing how long compromised or incorrectly issued certificates remain usable. Simply put, shorter certificate lifetimes mean attackers have less time to exploit a stolen private key.
>

title: ReactOS Can Now Be Installed & Used With Its NTFS Driver
body:
>The ReactOS open-source operating system has seen its NTFS file-system driver mature to the point that it can be finally used for installing and using ReactOS with it. NTFS formatting support is also finally now possible with this driver too.
>
>Hitting this major milestone of its NTFS driver maturing to the point of installing and using the ReactOS operating system itself with it also puts the project one step closer to its elusive beta release.
>
>ReactOS posted to X today this big goal being realized of the NTFS driver being much more mature for handling ReactOS installations.
>
>It is important to note though that the ReactOS NTFS driver still lacks caching leading to slower performance than other NTFS drivers/platforms, journaling, and security support are also not yet implemented. There is also the possibility of other undiscovered bugs they note.
>
>A nice milestone for ReactOS and the latest in a variety of nice achievements they have made so far in 2026.

title: Launch HN: Skillsync (YC W26) – AI chat sessions made portable across agents
body:
Hey HN, we're Nars & Nishant, founders of Skillsync (https://skillsync.com)

Skillsync lets you move your AI chats across every coding agent. Most of our work exists as conversations, which are currently scattered across our agents. Though stored locally, these conversations use different formats. This is annoying because you cannot simply switch between agents without starting over. We get locked into a single provider and their agent as we invest in skills and memories over time. Skillsync acts as a universal converter. It moves the entire session, including all the messages, reasoning and tool calls so you can pick up right where you left off.

Skillsync collects all your sessions in one place and makes them searchable. It breaks down what each session is carrying, including which loaded skills the agent is actually using, making stale context easy to spot. You can also create shared workspaces to sync sessions across your team. You can build your own closed loop systems. Everything runs locally except when you share to workspaces.

title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
body:
I have been researching what the ultimate diff tool would look like, based on actual diffs in open source repositories.

OmniDiff can diff: code (25 languages), config, images, PDFs, archives, cursors, fonts...

It's fast. It can diff C++ files of tens of thousands of lines in under 100ms, on a 2023 ThinkPad T14s.

It's open source. AGPLv3.

It's based on real diffs. I looked at the 7400 repositories that are listed in Gentoo packages, sampled 2000 diffs and solved them manually to get a good understanding of what is needed, before putting together the diff pipelines for each content type. Incidentally, this also forms the basis of the CI pipeline, so the robustness of the codebase is quite high.

I'm still developing it. It's v0.3.0 at this time. But I have been using it daily as my git difftool for months now, and it works well.

AI Disclosure: Yes, I do use AI. No, I do not vibecode.

title: Show HN: A language model that lives in a boot sector
body:
All the ideas came from the boot sector demo scene where people had been writing chess and BASIC games in 512 bytes, even a C compiler. I wondered what one can do using a neural network instead of a program and generating boot logs for non-existent hardware was something fun to try.

Entire inference engine is 510 bytes of MBR, weights, vocab, and strings reside in the sectors following MBR. Small char-level neural network was trained on dmesg generated by machine, so machine produces Linux boot messages infinitely.

I retrieved the hidden layer via QEMU’s debug port and compared the neurons' values with those of the simulator, one neuron at a time. Only the value of the first neuron was correct. title: Show HN: Overtone – Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape
body:
Hi HN, I'm Ruud, co-founder of Lont. We turn company emails into personalized videos.

Video captions cost us manual work twice: fixing misheard words, then fixing layout, like lines ending on “the”.

Overtone uses multiple models to listen to the audio: gpt-transcribe, Azure STT, and Elevenlabs Scribe. When they return conflicting results, Overtone sends small clips to the models again, and then lets an LLM decide what was actually said.

The LLM is like a human doing a sanity check on the transcription model. Humans would easily recognize a word to be different based on context. The LLM basically does the same, using an optional context prompt + its world knowledge. Because of this the Word Error Rate (WER) on many test files is lower when using Overtone, compared to just using a model without it.

Sure, the cost is higher because we use up to 3 different STT models + an LLM, but it still removes mistakes, reducing the time needed to fix captions to a minimum, and reducing the chance you'll miss something. For us it's worth it. For ultra high volume use cases it may not be.

title: Show HN: ADRs for AI – Deliberation records for human–AI work, versioned in Git
body:
Why is this worth your time? Essentially, this solves two problems of AI-assisted programming:

(a) the first problem is how to do oversight and what do oversight of and this is solved through the ORRCF (for Options, Recommendation, Rationale, Confidence, Falsifier) question format (in which models are supposed to surface all their doubts with fully fleshed out recommendations, with falsifier, to be approved or overridden)

(b) the second problem is how to scaffold sustainable AI-written code; the ADRs (Architectural Deliberation Records, after Nygard's decision records) written by the models, summarize all the thought process involved in any design decision and provides the blueprint for the code.

In tandem, the records provide both the reason why certain non-obvious design choices were made, from a constant, to a library choice, to an ordering in an operation; and also under what conditions different decisions would be made, for instance, in a different platform, or under different latency requirements, or for a different audience, and so on.

This is a framework I've been working for over a year, that is the starting point of all my projects.

title: Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents
body:
Hi HN! We’re Srikar and Kevan, founders of Alter – https://alterauth.com/. We’re building access control for agents that can take actions on behalf of multiple users.

If you’ve built an internal agent people use through Slack, you may have experienced this scenario: everyone signs in with their own account, but the agent connects to the CRM or billing system with one shared API key, so the agent can do anything that the key can do. User-level authentication in Slack does nothing to control what the agent can do in an external system like the CRM or billing system.

Here’s what Alter does:

-It acts as a proxy and manages downstream credentials for every API request that an agent takes;

-It takes identity into account for every action the agent does. Automatically take into account the end user identity of the person that the agent is taking actions on behalf of.

-It enforces fine grained runtime policies and records compliance grade audit logs.

title: Tell HN: I've been paying for a rural Tanzanian's education for 10 years
body:
Ten years ago I was 19 and traveling through East Africa, and I spent a summer in Ibumila, a village in the Njombe highlands of Tanzania. There's no school in the village. The nearest one is a boarding school an hour away that costs a few hundred dollars a year, which is out of reach for most families there and was about two weeks of summer job money for me. The daughter of the family I stayed with, Anwarite, was 11. I offered to pay her fees and told myself I'd keep paying as long as she wanted to keep going.

This summer she graduated from the University of Dar es Salaam with a degree in Language Studies, and last week she told me she'd been accepted into a Master of Arts in Swahili program there. Roughly 2% of people from Njombe ever finish a university degree. Her goal is to get a PhD and then to bring it back to the region.

Her entire 18-month master's program (tuition, registration, fees, books, supplies) comes to 3,060,000 TSh, about $1,161.

Alan Kay performs an improvisational avant garde layered audio feedback loop about Claude Shannon, live online during Kristen Nygaard's 100-year birthday celebration.

Alan was scheduled to talk about how encountering Simula sparked his early thoughts about objects. During setup, somebody had the live stream playing out loud near an open Zoom mic, so his own voice kept arriving back in his ears about 21 seconds late, over and over.

Shannon's noisy channel coding theorem is the math for exactly the kind of channel that was garbling him as he praised it.

title: Show HN: Check if any of the $656M in unclaimed royalties at The MLC is yours
body:
Hi HN, I built this. Quick background on why it exists:

When music is streamed on digital streaming platforms (think Spotify, Apple Music, Pandora), there are two separate royalty streams: one for the recording, paid through your distributor (DistroKid, TuneCore, CDBaby), and one for the underlying work (generally known as publishing). The work side's mechanical royalties are collected by The MLC, a nonprofit that was created by the 2018 Music Modernization Act (MMA). If you haven't registered your songs with The MLC, there are issues with your metadata, or about half a dozen other reasons, that money will never reach you, it just collects in a big pile we call the "black box".

That pile is big. The MLC's own dashboard currently shows over $656M is held (themlc.com/blanket-royalties), and the biggest problem is the MMA dictates that The MLC cannot hold that money indefinitely. At some point, by law, The MLC must distribute this big pile of cash, and since they don't know who it's supposed to go to, they pay it out through a process called "market share" (themlc.com/marketshare). It’s is rust native, built for concurrency, and implements all the config quirks across models and providers (streaming formats, tool calls, model parameters, rate limits, and different error behavior).

The gateway adds under 1 ms for BYOK requests and under 2 ms when Experiential supplies the provider key. It has every major inference provider, and 1000+ models refreshed daily via a codex agent that opens a PR.

Compared to other similar projects we’re open source, take no markup, allow you to mix local models with a marketplace, and use your traffic to (opt in) train you a model. Simple routing doesn’t warrant a 10% token markup.

The way we do this is given standardized OTel traces, we mine representative real tasks, use text world models to simulate rollouts for various models, apply an LLM judge, and fit a nearest neighbor classifier on top of an embedding of a prompt to decide the optimal model for each request.
